sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: One-step and few-step text-to-image generation must accurately render the details specified in the prompt despite limited opportunities for refinement. Distribution matching distillation (DMD) uses score differences to bring the generated distribution closer to a reference distribution. Following prior work, we estimate this difference with internal velocity branches, avoiding a separate fake-score network. We ask whether an explicit moment constraint improves this learned score supervision. A decomposition of the reverse-KL field into a Gaussian moment component and a non-Gaussian residual identifies statistics that can be constrained explicitly. We introduce Intrinsic Distribution Matching (IDM), which retains the full DMD correction and matches feature means and per-coordinate standard deviations using the generator's exponential-moving-average (EMA) copy, requiring no external feature encoder. Experiments use full-parameter and low-rank adaptation (LoRA) tuning on Z-Image-Turbo 6B and Qwen-Image 20B. At two network evaluations, IDM reaches 94.25% and 90.20% on Chinese and English LongText-Bench, the highest scores among the compared methods at this budget. Controlled ablations show gains from the added moment loss, while generator EMA features perform competitively with an external DINOv2 encoder across the five reported metrics. Code is available at https://github.com/inclusionAI/IDM.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Diffusion and flow-matching models produce high-quality images, but their repeated network evaluations impose substantial inference cost (Ho et al., 2020; Song et al., 2020; Lipman et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2023). One and few-step generation reduces this cost by learning much shorter sampling process. The challenge is to accurately render the details specified in the prompt using only one or few sampling steps. Long-text rendering makes this challenge concrete: many characters must remain legible and correct within coherent image (Geng et al., 2025b; Wu et al., 2025a). It therefore provides demanding test of whether fast generation retains detailed conditional information. Distribution matching distillation (DMD) trains fast generator to match reference distribution (Yin et al., 2024b;a). score describes the local direction of increasing log density. pretrained teacher supplies the reference score, while an auxiliary fake-score network estimates the score of the current generated distribution. Their difference guides updates to generated samples. These updates are applied sample by sample, but their direction depends on both distributions. Distribution matching can complement trajectory-based training: rCM combines score regularization with continuous-time consistency training (Zheng et al., 2025). TwinFlow and APEX obtain this score difference from internally separated velocity branches of the generator (Cheng et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026a). The model-score estimate is still learned, but no separate fake-score network is needed. We adopt this internal construction and ask whether the generator can also supply an explicit constraint on statistics across samples. Although the exact DMD field contains full distributional information, learned score estimates and finite training can leave discrepancies that an additional statistical objective may help reduce. Equal contribution. *Corresponding author. 1 Figure 1: Overview of IDM for one-step generation. Multi-step sampling refines samples iteratively, whereas one-step generation learns direct noise-to-data map. IDM combines an internal DMD loss with feature-moment loss in the generators EMA feature space. The right panel illustrates idealized alignment with single-evaluation inference. To motivate such constraint, we revisit the reverse-KL score difference underlying DMD. Building on the Gaussian-plus-residual score representation (Wang & Vastola, 2023; 2024), we separate component determined by means and covariances from the remaining score structure in Section 3.3 . This identifies statistics that can be constrained explicitly, while showing why moments alone do not determine the full distribution. We therefore retain the full DMD correction and add moment loss, testing its benefit through controlled ablations in shared training setting. We introduce Intrinsic Distribution Matching (IDM), which augments internal DMD with moment matching in the generators own feature space. Its exponential-moving-average (EMA) copy provides shared representation for generated and reference samples; we match the means and per-coordinate standard deviations of these features. Unlike objectives that obtain features from an external encoder or teacher (Yang et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026b), this design reuses the generator for both score estimation and feature extraction. Both training signals are obtained from the generator and its EMA copy, without separate discriminator, score model, or external feature encoder. We evaluate IDM using Z-Image-Turbo 6B and Qwen-Image 20B with full-parameter and LoRA tuning in Section 5 . LongText-Bench evaluates the Chinese and English long-text rendering fidelity emphasized above, with subsets denoted LongText-CN and LongText-EN (Geng et al., 2025b). At two network evaluations (2 NFE), IDM on Z-Image-Turbo achieves state-of-the-art scores among the compared methods: 94.25% and 90.20%, improving over Z-Image-Turbo++ by 2.63 and 0.32 percentage points, respectively in Table 5 . Our main contributions are: a. Intrinsic distributional supervision. We augment internal DMD with an explicit loss on the means and per-coordinate standard deviations of generator EMA features. This adds statistical supervision across samples without separate external feature encoder. b. Distribution-gradient explanation. Building on the Gaussian-plus-residual score representation, we motivate an explicit moment constraint alongside the full DMD correction. c. Few-step training and evaluation. We demonstrate full-parameter and LoRA training on 6B and 20B backbones. Ablations assess the added moment loss, EMA features, and regression choices, while LongText-Bench evaluates fine-grained text fidelity. 2 Figure 2: IDM (Z-Image), 2 NFE. Text rendering and portrait generation.

sections.content: Lpop over internal DMD, the suitability of generator EMA features Our experiments assess the added value of relative to an external encoder, and the choice of velocity and endpoint regression. System-level comparisons evaluate the complete training setting; controlled ablations examine these individual choices under the Lpop. shared data, backbone, and sampling budget. Throughout this section, Lpop refers to the empirical loss (cid:98) 5.1 Experimental Setup Backbones and tuning. We initialize IDM from Z-Image-Turbo 6B (Team, 2025) and Qwen-Image 20B (Wu et al., 2025a), using full-parameter tuning and LoRA with ranks 32 and 64. We denote the resulting models by IDM (Z-Image) and IDM (Qwen-Image); the former uses the Turbo checkpoint rather than the undistilled Z-Image base model. Training data. The reference data defining pr combine ShareGPT-4o (Chen et al., 2025c), BLIP-3o (Chen et al., 2025a), and samples synthesized with Qwen-Image-2512 and Z-Image-Turbo: 600K from FLUX-Reason-6M prompts (Fang et al., 2025) and 5M from text-rendering prompts. Compared with the 200K poster-prompt samples used by APEX (Liu et al., 2026a), this larger text-focused collection provides more training examples for dense text rendering. Training configuration. All models use BF16, FlashAttention4, and FSDP2 with global batch size 64. Training runs for 15K steps on Z-Image-Turbo 6B and 10K steps for Qwen-Image 20B LoRA, using 32 H100 A100 80GB GPUs. The default weights are λscore = 1 and λpop = 0.5, fixed throughout training. 80GB and 8 Each trained checkpoint is evaluated at both 1 and 2 NFE without changing the training loss weights for either sampling budget. Published reference results retain their training data and configuration; the internal IDM ablations use the shared configuration above. sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented Intrinsic Distribution Matching (IDM), which builds on internal DMD and adds an explicit constraint on generator EMA feature statistics. The reverse-KL field decomposition motivates retaining full score-difference supervision while additionally matching feature means and standard deviations. Controlled ablations show gains over the internal DMD baseline from EMA feature moments, with performance close to DINOv2. On Z-Image-Turbo 6B, IDM reaches 94.25% and 90.20% on Chinese and English LongText-Bench, the highest scores among the compared two-NFE methods. Experiments on backbones up to 20B parameters support using the generators predictions and representations together for few-step text-to-image generation.

Progressive distillation, consistency models, shortcut models, and MeanFlow reduce sampling steps by learning transitions or relations along generative trajectory (Salimans & Ho, 2022; Song et al., 2023; Lu & Song, 2024; Frans et al., 2024; Geng et al., 2025a; 2026). Duality Models jointly predict velocities and flow maps with shared backbone (Sun et al., 2026b). Distributional approaches use adversarial or score-based supervision to train generated outputs directly (Sauer et al., 2023; 2024; Yin et al., 2024b;a). rCM combines continuous-time consistency with score regularization and demonstrates their complementarity on large image and video models (Zheng et al., 2025). LLaDA-Image-Turbo supports inference in two to four steps, while Vidu S2 targets real-time interactive video generation and editing (Chen et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a). IDM studies distributional supervision from the generator itself. Distribution Gradients and Internal Score Estimation. DMD estimates the score difference between noised reference and generated distributions using reference network and an online fake-score model (Yin et al., 2024b); DMD2 adds adversarial supervision and techniques for stable few-step distillation (Yin et al., 2024a). Related work connects adversarial and score-based updates through sample-space fields (Franceschi et al., 2023; Weber, 2023) and extends distribution matching to broader divergence families (Xu et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026). FlowCPO develops an offline forward-KL formulation for preference alignment in flow models (Han et al., 2026b). TwinFlow and APEX estimate score differences through internally separated velocity branches (Cheng et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026a). IDM adds feature-moment loss to internal DMD. Feature-Space Distribution Matching. GMMN and MMD-GAN use moment or kernel discrepancies for generative training (Li et al., 2015; 2017). FD-Loss turns full-covariance Gaussian feature discrepancy into training objective and uses queue or EMA estimators to connect population statistics with batch gradients (Heusel et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2026). Three-Body Scattering derives one-step regression targets from energy-distance interactions in frozen features (Sun et al., 2026a). Drifting and W-Flow construct distributional updates through kernel interactions and batchwise optimal transport, respectively (Deng et al., 2026; Han et al., 2026a), while Teacher-Feature Drifting uses representations from pretrained teacher (Zhang et al., 2026b). IDM instead matches feature means and per-coordinate standard deviations in the generators EMA feature space. Gaussian Score Structure and Intrinsic Representations. The Gaussian-plus-residual score representation of Wang & Vastola (2023; 2024) underlies our reverse-KL field decomposition and motivates an additional feature-moment constraint. REPA shows that diffusion-transformer hidden states contain useful semantic information and can be strengthened through external representation alignment (Yu et al., 2024). Embedded Representation Warmup adds dedicated representation-alignment stage before generative training (Liu et al., 2025). Our EMA feature map reuses such internal representations and evolves with the generator; its utility is evaluated against external, teacher, and live self-feature alternatives in Section 5.3 . Text Rendering in Image Generation. Recent text-to-image models, including Qwen-Image and X-Omni, place increasing emphasis on accurate text rendering (Wu et al., 2025a; Geng et al., 2025b). LongText-Bench evaluates extended Chinese and English text across multiple scenarios (Geng et al., 2025b), complementing the broader dimensions assessed by OneIG (Chang et al., 2026). Z-Image-Turbo++ reports LongText as sensitive measure of text quality under limited sampling budget (Liu et al., 2026b). We focus on LongText performance at 2 NFE.
